fields.title: User story: all the value is in the "so that" part
fields.keyTakeaway: The value of the statement lies in the "so that" ending. If you cannot fill it in honestly, you are describing a feature, not a task, and you'll have no way to verify the result.
fields.checkQuestion: "As a dispatcher, I want an export to Excel button, so that there is an export to Excel." What's wrong here?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node: **what tasks will users solve?** There is a gulf between "we need a car filter" and "we need to see who is available on Thursday within a minute." You can build the former literally and miss the mark.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer this question.** The team builds screens, not tasks. Each screen individually matches a request, but together they don't form the job a person came to do.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: As a <role>, I want <action>, so that <benefit>
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Role**—not a job title, but a person in a specific situation.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Action**—what they do, not an interface element.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **So that**—why; this is the only part you can verify after release.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: A story is not a document, but a **promise of a conversation**. It reminds you to talk rather than replacing the conversation.
fields.blocks/3/items/0: "As a dispatcher, I want a filter button" → "As a dispatcher, I want to see available cars for a selected date, so that I don't have to call drivers one by one"
fields.blocks/3/items/1: "As an accountant, I want an export" → "As an accountant, I want to get monthly hours for each driver, so that I don't have to compile them manually"
fields.blocks/3/items/2: "As a director, I want a dashboard" → "As a director, I want to see vehicle downtime once a week, so that I can decide if we need another vehicle"
fields.blocks/4/text: Notice that after rewriting, each story gets a **method of verification**: number of calls, time to compile hours, purchase decision. Formulations with a button or dashboard lack this method.
fields.blocks/5/text:
The story "as a dispatcher, I want to reassign a trip so that I can cover a driver rejection" looks simple right up to the first question: what if the new driver doesn't have enough labor hours? What if the car is a different class? What if the cargo is already loaded?

Here you need a Use Case—a sequence of steps with explicit alternatives and exceptions. The rule is simple: **a story describes intent, a use case describes branching**. As soon as there are more than two branches and they are costly, a user story is no longer enough.
fields.blocks/5/title: Dispetcher: where a Use Case is actually needed
fields.blocks/6/text: A template doesn't make a story good. "As a user, I want to use the system so that I solve tasks" is formally correct and useless. And don't describe everything with stories: permissions setup, data migration, integration—these are tasks with no user intent, and pretending otherwise is harmful.
